body.heading: Care is mostly logistics
paragraphs: In a shared household, love shows up as labour: the appointment booked, the bins out, the child's shoes found, the car filled with fuel. Each act is small enough to miss, and together they are most of the evidence that someone is looking after you.

Because the acts are small, they are easy to stop seeing. The person doing them can feel like staff rather than a partner — not because anyone is ungrateful, but because the work has become the wallpaper.

body.heading: Train the noticing
paragraphs: Make a private game of it for a week: catch three things a day that your partner did for the household or for you, and mention at least one of them. Mentioning is the step that matters; unspoken gratitude benefits only the thinker.
Be specific about the invisible kinds especially: remembering, organising, worrying ahead, smoothing things with relatives. The mental load is real work, and naming it is a form of sharing it.

body.heading: Noticing changes the noticer
paragraphs: People who practise noticing usually report a side effect: their own contribution feels more seen too, partly because the household's whole economy of care has become a topic instead of a background. What gets mentioned gets valued; what gets valued gets shared more fairly.
It works with children, colleagues, and parents too. Anyone whose care has become wallpaper brightens when it is finally described back to them.

description: Most care in a relationship is small, daily, and easy to stop seeing — noticing it out loud keeps it visible and valued.
